title: Finite Element Modeling of Fracture in Brittle Foods with Physically Consistent Parameter Calibration: A Practical Case Study on Cooled Dark Chocolate
authors: Patrick Kurzeja, Felix Rörentrop, Kai Langenfeld, Jörn Mosler
abstract: Fracture in food can be undesired during production and transportation but also intended during cutting, grinding or mastication. The associated peak load, the deformation at failure and the resulting fragment geometry are all product properties. This work condenses the modeling of such fracture into a physically rigorous recipe that considers the practical constraints imposed by finite element simulations where necessary and applies idealized theoretical assessments where applicable. Cooled dark chocolate serves as a reproducible model material. Two well-established modeling frameworks for Griffith-type brittle fracture are assessed at an affordable spatial discretization: a sharp-interface and a diffuse phase-field approach. The assessment covers the choice of numerical framework, its discretization and a staged identification of the model parameters. Each parameter is identified from the loading stage that governs it: elastic parameters from pre-crack tension and compression, critical energy release rate from three-point-bending peak force, and the phase-field width last. The phase-field width interferes with the structural response, crack curvature and stress fields, depending on its lower bound set by the affordable spatial resolution. Elastic slope, peak force and crack path therefore cannot be met practically by a single parameter set. The objective must be fixed for the calibration of the model parameters and reported together with the numerical parameters and the boundary value problem.

infographic.key_insight: At affordable mesh resolution, a single phase-field parameter set cannot simultaneously match elastic slope, peak force, and crack path in brittle chocolate fracture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable fracture predictions for food processing and handling require calibration to a declared objective, with numerical settings and boundary conditions reported.
method: Compare sharp-interface and diffuse phase-field frameworks for Griffith-type fracture in cooled dark chocolate.
Identify elastic parameters from pre-crack tension and compression, then critical energy release rate from three-point-bending peak force.
Calibrate phase-field width last, accounting for mesh-resolution constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The assessment uses tension, compression, and three-point bending to examine parameter calibration, while evaluating how phase-field width affects structural response, crack curvature, and stress fields.
infographic.watch_item: Mesh-limited phase-field width can alter predicted fracture behavior, so calibration must target a specified observable rather than assume simultaneous agreement across all outputs.
infographic.paper_title: Finite Element Modeling of Fracture in Brittle Foods with Physically Consistent Parameter Calibration: A Practical Case Study on Cooled Dark Chocolate

title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity
authors: Yue Wu, Yuan Tian, Deng Pan, Mingwei Chen
abstract: Adapting a pre-trained machine-learning interatomic potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity requires improving defect accuracy without degrading the near-equilibrium elastic and vibrational response. Here we achieve this balance for the aluminium MACE potential QP17 by integrating conditional readout uncertainty, iterative full-parameter updates and protocol-compatible relative-energy anchoring. Sensitivities over 144 linear readout weights guide acquisition, with within-batch covariance updates and evolving neural representations. After four active-learning rounds (32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates), force-uncertainty acquisition reduces mean development force error from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Angstrom, outperforming random sampling (22.70), geometry-diversity selection (22.46) and uniform training across all 104 candidate labels (22.71) under the same update budget. All three force-uncertainty runs satisfy bulk-mechanical retention criteria: historical relative-energy error decreases from 0.375 to 0.207 meV/atom, while harmonic phonon root-mean-square drift remains below 0.05 THz. Matched objective ablations reveal that relative-energy anchoring suppresses harmonic drift. Out-of-sample evaluations across planar faults, twin boundaries and grain boundaries demonstrate transferable gains in defect energies and deviatoric stresses, even though virial stresses are never fitted. A closed-loop molecular dynamics and density functional theory (MD-DFT) pilot confirms that automated acceptance gating intercepts updates that violate historical elastic-group energy or vibrational tolerances. Together, these components establish a retention-constrained fine-tuning protocol for improving plastic-deformation observables while preserving the tested bulk mechanical response.

infographic.key_insight: Retention-constrained fine-tuning improves an aluminium MACE potential’s defect predictions while preserving its tested near-equilibrium mechanical and vibrational response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports atomistic simulations of plasticity with better defect energetics and stresses without sacrificing validated bulk behavior.
method: Select configurations using conditional force uncertainty, with within-batch covariance updates.
Iteratively update all model parameters while anchoring historical relative energies.
Gate updates against historical elastic-group energy and vibrational tolerances.
infographic.evidence_signal: After 32 acquired configurations and 400 gradient updates, mean development force error fell from 22.43 to 21.52 meV/Å, outperforming sampling baselines; all three force-uncertainty runs met retention criteria, with harmonic phonon RMS drift below 0.05 THz.
infographic.watch_item: Retention is demonstrated for tested aluminium benchmarks; new deformation regimes require additional validation and compatible reference-energy protocols.
infographic.paper_title: Retention-constrained fine-tuning of a pre-trained aluminium MACE potential for non-equilibrium defect dynamics and plasticity

title: Total Deformation-based MPM for Perfectly Elastic Solid Simulation with Strong Deformations
authors: Timna Böttcher, Rick Ridder, Jan Bender
abstract: We present a new MPM-based solver for perfectly elastic solids, which can recover from strong deformations and naturally allows contact handling. Typical MPM solvers suffer from numerical fracture, where objects break apart even when no plasticity is included in the elasticity model. Previous approaches for perfectly elastic solids solve this by computing forces on a fixed grid in the reference configuration. However, this makes them incompatible with standard collision handling methods. We instead propose a method for deformable solid simulation without numerical fracture, that still computes elastic forces on the current grid. Our method can easily include grid-based collision handling, as commonly used in MPM frameworks. Additionally, we compute the deformation directly from the particle positions and a fixed reference grid, without any updates based on velocity gradients. This facilitates the inclusion of particle-level collision handling and zero-energy mode suppression, which counteracts artifacts from non-linear deformations. As a result, we can efficiently simulate complex scenarios of elastic objects undergoing large deformations, including contact.

infographic.key_insight: Total deformation-based MPM prevents numerical fracture in perfectly elastic solids while computing elastic forces on the current grid for contact handling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports simulation of elastic components undergoing large, recoverable deformations and contact without artificial breakup.
method: Compute deformation directly from particle positions using a fixed reference grid.
Evaluate elastic forces on the current grid, retaining standard grid-based collision handling.
Support particle-level collision handling and zero-energy mode suppression.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports efficient simulations of complex elastic objects under large deformations and contact, but provides no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness and computational overhead of the fixed-reference deformation calculation and zero-energy mode suppression require assessment beyond the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Total Deformation-based MPM for Perfectly Elastic Solid Simulation with Strong Deformations

title: A minimizing-movement framework for parametric finite element approximation of anisotropic curve shortening flows
authors: Wei Jiang, Chunmei Su, Ganghui Zhang
abstract: We propose a minimizing-movement framework for constructing parametric finite element methods (PFEMs) for anisotropic curve shortening flows. The cornerstone is an admissible modified energy: a smooth, convex, and iteration-dependent surrogate that majorizes the original anisotropic energy and agrees with it at the current iterate. For any fixed finite element degree $n\geq1$ and any positive surface energy density $γ\in C^2(\mathbb{S}^1)$, the unconstrained one-step problem has a unique solution for any time-step size whenever the parametric derivative of the current discrete curve does not vanish on any mesh element. It also satisfies a one-step discrete energy dissipation inequality. It therefore preserves the variational structure of the underlying $L^2$-gradient flow. The framework recovers a variational interpretation of Dziuk's isotropic scheme and applies directly to the weak anisotropies. For strong anisotropies, a convex splitting removes the weak-anisotropy restriction on the original density. A scalar constraint further extends the framework to area-preserving flows. Numerical experiments exhibit approximately the expected convergence for smooth isotropic and weakly anisotropic examples. They also confirm energy dissipation and area preservation. In the strongly anisotropic regime, the computations produce sharp facet-like profiles but reveal mesh-scale oscillations under the grid refinement.

infographic.key_insight: A minimizing-movement framework uses a convex surrogate energy to construct parametric finite element schemes with unique one-step solutions and discrete energy dissipation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports energy-consistent simulation of anisotropic interface motion, including area-preserving evolution relevant to materials microstructure modeling.
method: Majorize the anisotropic energy with a smooth, convex surrogate matching it at the current iterate.
Minimize at each time step using parametric finite elements of any fixed degree.
Use convex splitting for strong anisotropy and a scalar constraint for area preservation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments show approximately expected convergence in smooth isotropic and weakly anisotropic cases, energy dissipation, and area preservation.
infographic.watch_item: Strongly anisotropic tests develop mesh-scale oscillations under refinement; one-step uniqueness also requires a nonvanishing current-curve derivative on every element.
infographic.paper_title: A minimizing-movement framework for parametric finite element approximation of anisotropic curve shortening flows

title: Evaluation of upper-scale mechanical parameters of particulate aluminum-based nanocomposites from molecular simulations
authors: Bartosz Bucholc, Marcin Maździarz, Szymon Nosewicz
abstract: This paper focuses on the numerical and analytical determination of the mechanical parameters of aluminum-matrix nanocomposites using atomistic-scale simulations within a multiscale modeling framework. Molecular statics simulations were employed to evaluate the tensile and compressive behavior of Al based composites reinforced with nanosized alumina particles. Two classes of atomistic models were investigated. First, a unit-cell model containing a single Al2O3 monocrystal embedded in an aluminum matrix was used to examine the influence of the volume fraction of the ceramic inclusion on the effective mechanical properties. Second, a polycrystalline RVE model comprising an alumina particle was analyzed to assess the effect of the number of Al grains on effective properties. For each case, the mechanical response was characterized by stress-strain curves, enabling the identification of upper-scale material parameters associated with the elastic regime (bulk, shear and Young's modulus) and the damage stage (ultimate strength, ultimate strain, and failure strain). The isotropized elastic constants evaluated from molecular simulations were compared with classical Voigt-Reuss-Hill bounds to assess their applicability in the elastic regime. Finally, atomistic-scale simulation outputs provided insight into the dominant deformation/damage mechanisms (brittle versus ductile) and fracture modes (transgranular versus intergranular).

infographic.key_insight: Atomistic simulations link alumina inclusion fraction and aluminum grain structure to effective elastic properties, strength, and fracture behavior in aluminum-based nanocomposites.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports multiscale material modeling by extracting upper-scale mechanical parameters from nanoscale composite responses.
method: Run molecular statics simulations under tensile and compressive loading.
Compare single-inclusion unit cells with polycrystalline representative volume elements containing an alumina particle.
Extract elastic and damage parameters from stress–strain curves and compare isotropized elastic constants with Voigt–Reuss–Hill estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation of bulk, shear, and Young’s moduli, ultimate strength, ultimate strain, and failure strain, alongside analysis of ductile/brittle mechanisms and intergranular/transgranular fracture.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative accuracy or experimental validation, so transfer of atomistic parameters to engineering-scale predictions requires further assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluation of upper-scale mechanical parameters of particulate aluminum-based nanocomposites from molecular simulations

title: Constrained neural softening functions for the Mullins effect in parameter-dependent materials
authors: Dominik K. Klein, Jonas Fey, Maximilian Kannapinn, Oliver Weeger
abstract: Accurately capturing the Mullins effect across varying material compositions remains challenging, as constitutive models must unify flexible representations of stress softening with physical consistency and robust parameter calibration. In this work, we investigate parameter-dependent physics-augmented neural network constitutive models within the pseudo-elastic modeling framework, focusing on structural constraints that ensure physically admissible neural softening functions. This paper has three key contributions: (1) We formulate different neural softening functions within the pseudo-elastic framework, including a multiplicative decomposition of the softening function that enables parameter-dependent ansatz functions satisfying common mechanical constitutive conditions by construction. (2) We derive a sufficient condition for ellipticity of pseudo-elastic constitutive models, which can be enforced in the constitutive models by construction. (3) We systematically investigate how flexibility and structural constraints influence the performance of neural softening functions in terms of prediction accuracy and calibration robustness. For this, we consider multiaxial experimental data of carbon black-filled EPDM rubber synthesized with varying amounts of curatives. The findings of our work suggest that neural softening functions are a promising extension of the classical pseudo-elastic framework and, when subject to suitable constraints, can improve predictive accuracy for highly nonlinear, parameter-dependent materials.

infographic.key_insight: Structurally constrained neural softening functions extend pseudo-elastic Mullins models to capture composition-dependent stress softening while preserving physical admissibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve constitutive predictions for filled rubber formulations whose nonlinear response varies with curative content.
method: Embed parameter-dependent, physics-augmented neural softening functions in a pseudo-elastic framework.
Use multiplicative softening decompositions to satisfy mechanical constraints by construction.
Derive an enforceable sufficient condition for ellipticity and assess constraint–flexibility trade-offs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses multiaxial experimental data from carbon black-filled EPDM rubber with varying curative amounts to assess prediction accuracy and calibration robustness.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the tested formulations and loading conditions is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Constrained neural softening functions for the Mullins effect in parameter-dependent materials

title: A hyper-reduction strategy for elastoplastic hydro-mechanical problems in partially saturated soil
authors: Alba Muixí, Lluís Monforte, Antonio Rodríguez-Ferran, Sergio Zlotnik
abstract: This work proposes a hyper-reduced order model for coupled hydro-mechanical simulations of elastoplastic deformation and water flow in partially saturated soils. These simulations are used to monitor and assess the safety of geotechnical structures such as earthfill dams, where calibration, uncertainty quantification and scenario analysis require solving the same transient model many times for different parameter values. The displacement and the pore pressure are approximated in a field-split reduced basis obtained by proper orthogonal decomposition, and the Galerkin-projected equations are integrated with decomposed cubature rules, one per balance equation, built with the energy-conserving sampling and weighting (ECSW) method. Each residual is split into an affine part and a nonlinear correction: the affine part is computed exactly, at negligible online cost, so that the cubature rule only needs to approximate the correction, which is localized in space. The construction is independent of the constitutive model choices and is implemented in FEniCSx by assembling the original variational forms on the small set of elements selected by ECSW. The method is tested on two- and three-dimensional dams retaining tailings and water, simulating a raise of the dam and the subsequent consolidation phase, with the friction angle, stiffness and hydraulic conductivity of the dam material and the height of the raise as varying parameters. The hyper-reduced model reproduces the displacement and pressure fields with errors below $0.5\%$ with respect to the finite element solution, achieving speed-ups of up to $43\times$ in two dimensions and $77\times$ in three. These performance gains grow with the extent of the plastic yielding, and the selected elements concentrate in the plastified and unsaturated zones, whose size is set by the physics rather than by the mesh resolution.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-localized hyper-reduction preserves coupled soil displacement and pore-pressure predictions while accelerating elastoplastic hydro-mechanical simulations by up to 77×.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster repeated simulations can support calibration, uncertainty quantification and scenario analysis for partially saturated earthfill and tailings dams.
method: Build separate displacement and pore-pressure reduced bases using proper orthogonal decomposition.
Evaluate affine residual terms exactly and approximate nonlinear corrections using one ECSW cubature rule per balance equation.
Assemble the original FEniCSx variational forms only on ECSW-selected elements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on 2D and 3D dams undergoing raising and consolidation, with varying material parameters and raise height, reported field errors below 0.5% relative to finite elements and speed-ups up to 43× and 77×, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy beyond the tested parameter ranges and loading scenarios remains unestablished; new yielding or unsaturated zones may require updated training and element selection.
infographic.paper_title: A hyper-reduction strategy for elastoplastic hydro-mechanical problems in partially saturated soil

title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes
authors: Florian Gammer
abstract: Symmetric polyconvexity provides a sufficient condition for weak lower semicontinuity in small-strain elasticity and a tractable lower bound for the relaxation of non-(quasi)convex energies. Since classical algorithms for computing such functions can be computationally expensive, neural network approximations have recently emerged as an alternative. A central difficulty with establishing such neural network based approaches for symmetric polyconvexity is the additional monotonicity property. As we show, the corresponding weight restrictions on ReLU-based input-convex networks do not yield universal approximation of the lifted representers. Here, we introduce symmetric polyconvex neural networks (SPCNNs) for constitutive modeling and approximation of symmetric polyconvex envelopes. The deep architecture combines convexity with the monotonicity required of a representer in the space of minors. We prove a universal approximation theorem for symmetric polyconvex energies, without requiring isotropy, and quantify the number of affine pieces attainable by the lifted network and derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies. Numerical examples illustrate stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential. Symmetric polyconvexity is guaranteed by construction, while the accuracy of the fitted energies and envelopes is assessed numerically.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetric polyconvex neural networks guarantee symmetric polyconvexity by construction and universally approximate symmetric polyconvex energies without assuming isotropy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports learned small-strain constitutive models and approximation of symmetric polyconvex envelopes, which provide lower bounds for energy relaxation.
method: Combine convexity with the required monotonicity in a lifted space of minors.
Prove universal approximation beyond the limitations of weight-restricted ReLU input-convex networks.
Quantify attainable affine pieces and derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical examples assess stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential.
infographic.watch_item: Symmetric polyconvexity is guaranteed, but fitted accuracy is assessed numerically and the envelope need not equal the fully relaxed energy.
infographic.paper_title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes

title: ARISE: Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement for Continual Multimodal Forgery Detection
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Yaxiong Wang, Yujiao Wu, Lianwei Wu, Qi Zhang, Li Zhu
abstract: Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as generators, editing systems, and multimodal large language models continually introduce new forgery mechanisms and forensic evidence. We formulate this problem as attack-incremental continual multimodal forgery detection, where the binary real/fake interface remains fixed while emerging attacks must be learned without forgetting previous ones. We introduce Fable-Bench, which organizes attack evolution through complementary joint-modality, text-side, and image-side protocols. We further propose ARISE (Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement), motivated by the open-ended forged class and the comparatively reusable geometry of authentic content. ARISE fits a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations as a compact historical reference. Meanwhile, the proposed Gaussian-Responsibility-Aware Stability Preservation (GRASP) derives a sample-adaptive anisotropic metric that strongly constrains historically stable representation directions while retaining plasticity elsewhere. Our Vulnerability-Aware Replay (VAR) further estimates stage-wise vulnerability from authentic-density degradation, forged-to-authentic boundary confusion, and authentic-mode occupancy drift, then assigns bounded replay emphasis to fragile stages. All adaptive signals are obtained from training-time replay statistics, while inference uses only the original multimodal backbone and binary classification head. Experiments across three attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures demonstrate improved historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.

infographic.key_insight: ARISE uses authentic-content reference geometry to learn emerging multimodal forgery attacks while reducing forgetting of earlier attacks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets continually updated multimodal forensic systems, not solid mechanics or constitutive modeling.
method: Fit a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations.
Use GRASP to preserve historically stable representation directions while allowing adaptation elsewhere.
Use VAR to emphasize vulnerable historical stages based on training-time replay statistics, without adding inference modules.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved historical retention and final average performance across three Fable-Bench attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Effectiveness may depend on how well the replay buffer and Gaussian mixture capture authentic-content diversity.
infographic.paper_title: ARISE: Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement for Continual Multimodal Forgery Detection

title: Generative Replay for Equilibrium Propagation: Toward Edge-Friendly Continual Learning in Hopfield Networks
authors: Victor Cook, Gilles Sassatelli, Thierry Gil, Mohamed Watfa, Marina Reyboz
abstract: Equilibrium Propagation (EqProp) offers a biologically grounded and hardware-aligned alternative to backpropagation for training Hopfield Networks. However, its behavior in continual learning settings remains largely unexplored. This work confronts catastrophic forgetting in EqProp-trained Hopfield Networks from the inside out, eliminating the need for external data buffers or architectural overhead that standard Experience Replay \textbf{(ER)} and Generative Replay \textbf{(Gen-Replay)} inevitably require. We introduce an Energy-Based Generative Replay strategy \textbf{(EB-Gen)} which exploits the intrinsic generative dynamics of Hopfield Networks, allowing a single model to act as both classifier and replay samples generator. Samples capturing past task knowledge are generated by relaxing a frozen copy of the network, enabling rehearsal solely through internally generated pseudo-data. We evaluate the proposed method in the Class-Incremental setting, using the split versions of the MNIST and CIFAR10 benchmarks and compare it with FineTune, Experience Replay, Generative Replay, Sleep-Like Replay Consolidation (SRC) and Joint training. Our results show that EB-Gen significantly improves stability while preserving plasticity, achieving a 75\% and 64\% average accuracy on Split MNIST and Split CIFAR10 respectively. These findings show that Equilibrium Propagation can be adapted to alleviate catastrophic forgetting without forgoing the traits which made it compelling in the first place.

infographic.key_insight: Energy-Based Generative Replay (EB-Gen) reduces catastrophic forgetting by using Hopfield network dynamics to generate rehearsal samples internally.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support edge-friendly continual learning, though the abstract reports image-classification benchmarks rather than solid-mechanics applications.
method: Train a Hopfield network using Equilibrium Propagation.
Generate past-task pseudo-data by relaxing a frozen copy of the network.
Rehearse generated samples while learning new classes, without an external data buffer or separate generator architecture.
infographic.evidence_signal: Class-incremental evaluations report average accuracies of 75% on Split MNIST and 64% on Split CIFAR10, with comparisons against FineTune, ER, Gen-Replay, SRC and Joint training.
infographic.watch_item: Maintaining a frozen network copy and generating replay samples still incur memory and computation costs; edge-hardware efficiency is not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Replay for Equilibrium Propagation: Toward Edge-Friendly Continual Learning in Hopfield Networks

title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins
authors: Pablo Luna Falcon, Jason Mayeur, Amirkoushyar Ziabari, Vincent Paquit, Patxi Fernandez-Zelaia
abstract: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) offers substantial advantages to the fabrication of complex structural components, but its widespread adoption is slowed due to complexities in the process-structure-property relations which is the cause for uncertainty and drives risk. Accurately quantifying these complex relations solely via experimental workflows is time consuming and costly. Integrated computational materials and engineering (ICME) frameworks address this challenge by leveraging advanced computational tools, such as crystal plasticity finite element models (CPFEM), to predict critical mechanical properties directly from microstructural data. However, these frameworks require a large datasets that are often difficult to obtain, and their predictive accuracy depends on the availability of realistic AM microstructure representations. Generative deep learning models are a promising approach towards synthesizing AM microstructures which contain complex morphological and crystallographic features. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), in particular, show a strong potential to capture the inherent complexities of AM structures. In this work, we demonstrate that DDPMs can reliably synthesize digital-twin orientation-imaging micrographs, and we support this claim with quantitative evidence of the fidelity of the generated samples. Additionally, we establish a classifier-free guidance framework for solving complex inverse problems such as property-to-structure and process-to-structure mappings, and we showcase a potential application on a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification problem. Our work highlights the potential of AI-based generative modeling as a key component of computational frameworks for accelerating AM materials qualification and certification.

infographic.key_insight: Denoising diffusion models generate realistic additive-manufacturing microstructure images and enable inverse mappings from properties or process conditions to structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Synthetic microstructures could support crystal-plasticity simulations and uncertainty quantification to accelerate qualification of additively manufactured metals.
method: Train diffusion models to synthesize digital-twin orientation-imaging micrographs.
Use classifier-free guidance for property-to-structure and process-to-structure inverse mapping.
Demonstrate a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification application.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative evidence of generated-sample fidelity but provides no dataset sizes, evaluation metrics, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Image fidelity alone does not establish accurate downstream mechanical-property predictions; validation with crystal-plasticity simulations and experiments remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins

title: Co-Optimization of Network Topology and Variable Impedance Devices under Dynamic Line Ratings Using Iterative McCormick Relaxation
authors: Junseon Park, Hyeongon Park, Rahul K. gupta
abstract: Grid Enhancing Technologies (GETs), such as Network Topology Optimization (NTO), Dynamic Line Rating (DLR), and Variable Impedance Devices (VIDs) are increasingly deployed in power transmission grids to address congestion and improve grid utilization. However, their growing adoption necessitates coordinated operation to fully exploit their benefits. This paper presents a unified co-optimization framework that integrates NTO, DLR, and VID to alleviate congestion and minimize operational costs. NTO is modeled using a node-breaker formulation to provide enhanced switching granularity, while DLR incorporates weather-dependent parameters, including wind speed and ambient temperature, to dynamically adjust transmission limits. The resulting formulation is a mixed-integer nonlinear program due to power flow constraints with bilinear VID terms, and discrete topology decisions. To improve tractability, we propose using a McCormick relaxation approach to linearize bilinear terms. Furthermore, we propose an iterative refinement of the McCormick relaxation scheme to enhance solution accuracy. The proposed framework is validated through detailed analyses on the IEEE 118-bus system, along with additional case studies on other benchmark systems to assess scalability. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach improves solution accuracy compared to standard McCormick relaxation, achieves solution quality close to the nonlinear formulation, and maintains computational efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: Co-optimizing network topology, dynamic line ratings, and variable impedance devices can reduce grid congestion and operating costs while retaining computational tractability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps transmission operators coordinate grid-enhancing technologies to better utilize existing infrastructure.
method: Model topology switching with a node-breaker formulation and adjust line limits using weather-dependent ratings.
Jointly optimize discrete topology decisions and variable impedance settings.
Iteratively refine McCormick relaxations of bilinear terms to improve solution accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on the IEEE 118-bus system and other benchmarks report better accuracy than standard McCormick relaxation, solution quality close to the nonlinear formulation, and computational efficiency.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical accuracy or runtime results, so practical scalability and relaxation error require further assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Co-Optimization of Network Topology and Variable Impedance Devices under Dynamic Line Ratings Using Iterative McCormick Relaxation

title: Stiffness coefficients in granular micromechanics determined with three-point bending experiments and digital image correlation for a bimodulus material
authors: Mohammad Mahdi Nayeban, Bilen Emek Abali, Reza Afshar, Francesco Fabbrocino, Anil Misra, Luca Placidi
abstract: This study presents an inverse analysis to determine the stiffness parameters of a bimodulus constitutive model formulated within a granular micromechanics framework. Full-field normal strain measurements are obtained by Digital Image Correlation (DIC) during three-point bending tests and are used as experimental input to a hybrid numerical optimization procedure. The experimental campaign is designed to ensure that the measured strain fields remain within the elastic regime. Since the identification is formulated as a nonlinear regression problem, a physically informed initial parameter set is constructed to guide the optimization toward mechanically meaningful values. An initial estimate of the compressive stiffness is first obtained from the available manufacturer data. The tension-compression stiffness asymmetry is then estimated from the experimentally measured neutral-axis shift, which provides a macroscopic signature of bimodulus material behavior in bending. These estimates define the initial parameter set, which is subsequently refined through a hybrid optimization procedure based on the full-field comparison of the experimental and numerical normal strain distributions. The identified parameter set enables the numerical model to reproduce more closely both the through-depth profile and the spatial distribution of the normal strain component over the selected surface region. These results demonstrate that full-field normal strain measurements provide an effective basis for identifying the stiffness parameters of bimodulus granular micromechanics models. The largest differences between the numerical and experimental strain fields are observed near the load-application region, where localized strain variations are induced by the concentrated load.

infographic.key_insight: Full-field bending strains can identify tension–compression stiffness asymmetry in a bimodulus granular micromechanics model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports more faithful elastic bending simulations of materials with different tensile and compressive stiffnesses.
method: Measure full-field normal strains using digital image correlation during elastic three-point bending.
Initialize compressive stiffness from manufacturer data and stiffness asymmetry from the measured neutral-axis shift.
Refine stiffness parameters through hybrid optimization matching numerical and experimental strain fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: The identified parameters improved agreement with measured through-depth strain profiles and spatial strain distributions over the selected surface region.
infographic.watch_item: The largest strain-field discrepancies occur near the concentrated load, warranting caution when evaluating local predictions there.
infographic.paper_title: Stiffness coefficients in granular micromechanics determined with three-point bending experiments and digital image correlation for a bimodulus material

title: No friction required: Self-locking in entangled assemblies of curved filaments
authors: Benjamin R. Greenvall, Jay van den Berg, Ross E. Meinhart, Patrick A. Staudenmayer, Alfred J. Crosby, Gregory M. Grason
abstract: Filaments are incredible material building blocks that, when entangled together, form robust structures with remarkable adaptive mechanics, from stiff cables to stretchable knits. Basic questions about the mechanism that holds together such structures, especially assemblies like rope, without attractive physical or chemical bonds between constituents are among the oldest considered in materials science. Contradicting a long-standing picture that structural integrity of rope-like assemblies rely on a combination of external loading and inter-filament friction to prevent spontaneous detangling (e.g. fraying of a cut rope), we demonstrate that assemblies of intrinsically-curved filaments can achieve structural integrity purely from the competition of elastic forces that resist shape-change and (traction-free) repulsive forces that prevent overlap. We analyze a friction-free model of assembly of intrinsically-helical filaments, and show that depending on filament number and preferred filament shape, overcrowding in the assemblies generate elastic pre-stresses that give rise to either self-locking entanglement or spontaneous detanglement through propagation of a soliton-like detanglement front through assemblies. We test a generalized fracture criterion for spontaneous detangling and confirm the role of shape-elastic costs to self-locking via experiment and simulation of frictional filaments, demonstrating a range of bundled structures which cannot be made self-locking for any value of friction. The mechanism of ``purely elastic cohesion" illuminated here sheds light on self-locking in a broader class of entangled structures, and further, offers design principles for new classes of active filament materials capable of stimuli-responsive assembly and disassembly.

infographic.key_insight: Entangled, intrinsically curved filaments can self-lock without friction through competing elastic shape-restoring forces and repulsive contact forces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Filament geometry and bundle size offer design levers for cohesive assemblies and potentially stimuli-responsive materials that assemble or disassemble.
method: Analyze a friction-free model of intrinsically helical filament assemblies.
Test a generalized fracture criterion for spontaneous detangling.
Use experiments and simulations with frictional filaments to probe elastic self-locking.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports self-locking or soliton-like detanglement depending on filament number and preferred shape, including bundled structures that cannot self-lock at any friction level.
infographic.watch_item: Self-locking is geometry-dependent; friction alone cannot compensate for all filament shapes and bundle configurations.
infographic.paper_title: No friction required: Self-locking in entangled assemblies of curved filaments

title: Evolution of microstructure and crystallographic texture in a novel Zr-4Nb-2Al alloy during hot rotary swaging
authors: Adam Strnad, Jana Šmilauerová, Josef Stráský, Lukáš Horák, Jan Čapek, Alžběta Endrychová
abstract: A multi-step induction-assisted hot rotary swaging route was developed for the novel dual-phase Zr-4Nb-2Al alloy to investigate the evolution of microstructure, crystallographic texture, and mechanical properties during sequential deformation. Phase-transformation temperatures determined by electrical resistivity measurements were used to select processing conditions in the single-phase $β$ field at 880°C and the $α+β$ field at 780°C. Induction heating with thermographic temperature control enabled reduction of the initial 12 mm rod to 6.3 mm, corresponding to a total area reduction of 72%. Swaging in the $β$ field refined millimetre-sized prior-$β$ grains to approximately 100 $μ$m, while subsequent cooling produced a fine lamellar $α+β$ microstructure. Further deformation in the $α+β$ field disrupted the lamellar structure, promoted globularisation and recrystallisation of the $α$ phase, and refined the $β$ phase. The microstructural evolution was accompanied by a pronounced $\langle 11\bar{2}0\rangle_α\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ fibre texture in the $α$ phase, whereas the $β$ phase exhibited predominantly $\langle 110\rangle_β\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ together with a $\langle 111\rangle_β\parallel\mathrm{SD}$ component. The phase constitution remained comparatively stable, with approximately 12-15 wt.% retained $β$ throughout processing. Subsequent $α+β$ swaging decreased the compressive yield strength from 1103 to 839 MPa while increasing plastic deformability, with a maximum fracture strain of 32%. Radial hardness heterogeneity was progressively eliminated. These results demonstrate that induction-assisted rotary swaging in selected phase fields provides an effective route for tailoring microstructure, texture, and mechanical response in dual-phase zirconium alloys.

infographic.key_insight: Sequential hot rotary swaging refined Zr-4Nb-2Al microstructure and developed strong crystallographic textures, trading compressive yield strength for greater plastic deformability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Phase-field-controlled swaging offers a route to tailor dual-phase zirconium rods while reducing radial hardness heterogeneity.
method: Use electrical resistivity to identify phase-transformation temperatures.
Apply induction-assisted swaging at 880°C in the β field and 780°C in the α+β field.
Track microstructure, texture, phase content, hardness, and compression response.
infographic.evidence_signal: A 72% area reduction refined prior-β grains from millimetre scale to approximately 100 µm; subsequent α+β swaging lowered compressive yield strength from 1103 to 839 MPa, with maximum fracture strain reaching 32%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports compression results but does not establish tensile, fatigue, or service-environment performance.
infographic.paper_title: Evolution of microstructure and crystallographic texture in a novel Zr-4Nb-2Al alloy during hot rotary swaging

title: A Posteriori Error Analysis of Finite Element Approximation to an Evolution Equation with a Positive-Type Memory Term
authors: Sandhya Mel, Amiya Kumar Pani, Gujji Murali Mohan Reddy
abstract: This paper develops reliable a posteriori error estimates for finite element approximation of an evolution equation with a positive-type memory kernels on bounded convex polygonal or polyhedral domains, including both smooth and weakly singular kernels. For the weakly singular kernel $t^{α-1}/Γ(α),\; 0<α<1,$ the model captures the transition from parabolic diffusion to wave propagation, recovering the corresponding limiting equations as $α\to0^+$ and $α\to1^-$, respectively, with the memory term governing the intermediate dynamics. The spatial discretization employs time-dependent finite element spaces, while the backward Euler method combined with numerical quadrature is used for time integration. A unified \emph{a posteriori} analysis is established for both semidiscrete and fully discrete approximations. Elliptic reconstruction yields optimal spatial error estimates, while a memory-lag estimate preserves the essential cancellation in the convolution term, yielding a first-order temporal estimator whose kernel dependence is characterized by its integral. The resulting estimators are robust, with constants independent of the final time, spatial mesh size, and time step. Their kernel dependence involves only computable quantities, avoiding exponential growth in time. Moreover, for the weakly singular kernel, the $α$-dependent factors remain uniformly bounded for $α\in(0,1).$ Numerical experiments on a convex domain validate the theoretical results, and a space-time adaptive algorithm is also demonstrated on an L-shaped domain featuring a corner singularity and two temporal layers.

infographic.key_insight: Reliable a posteriori error estimators quantify finite element errors in evolution equations with memory without exponential growth in time, while remaining uniformly bounded across the fractional-kernel parameter range.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These estimators can guide adaptive simulation of memory-dependent dynamics transitioning between diffusion and wave propagation.
method: Time-dependent finite element spaces with backward Euler time stepping and memory quadrature.
Elliptic reconstruction for optimal spatial error estimates.
Memory-lag analysis preserving convolution cancellation for first-order temporal estimation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on a convex domain validate the estimates, and space-time adaptivity is demonstrated on an L-shaped domain with a corner singularity and two temporal layers.
infographic.watch_item: The stated theory assumes convex polygonal or polyhedral domains; the nonconvex L-shaped example is an adaptive demonstration.
infographic.paper_title: A Posteriori Error Analysis of Finite Element Approximation to an Evolution Equation with a Positive-Type Memory Term

title: An unconditionally convergent BDF2-type finite element integrator for the inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation
authors: Michele Aldé, Hywel Normington, Dirk Praetorius, Michele Ruggeri
abstract: We propose and analyze a fully discrete numerical scheme to approximate solutions to the inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (iLLG) equation, a state-of-the-art model to describe the dynamics of the magnetization at subpicosecond time scales. The method employs first-order finite elements for the spatial discretization and the two-step backward differentiation formula (BDF2) for the time discretization, where the inertial term is treated by a convex combination of BDF2 and the backward Euler method. We prove well-posedness and unconditional stability of the scheme, and obtain explicit bounds for the error in the realization of the iLLG-inherent unit length constraint satisfied by the magnetization. Moreover, we derive the discrete energy law satisfied by the approximations, which resembles the inherent dissipative energy law of the model. Finally, with a constructive approach, we prove unconditional convergence of the approximations toward a weak solution of the problem. Numerical experiments assess the performance of the scheme and validate the theoretical findings.

infographic.key_insight: A BDF2-type finite element scheme for inertial magnetization dynamics is unconditionally stable and converges to a weak solution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports reliable simulation of subpicosecond magnetization dynamics relevant to ultrafast magnetic devices.
method: First-order finite elements in space and BDF2 time stepping.
Inertial term discretized using a convex combination of BDF2 and backward Euler.
Proves well-posedness, a discrete dissipative energy law, and explicit unit-length constraint error bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments assess scheme performance and validate theoretical findings, but the abstract provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Unconditional stability and convergence do not remove time-resolution requirements for accurately capturing ultrafast dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: An unconditionally convergent BDF2-type finite element integrator for the inertial Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation

title: Robust augmented Block Preconditioning for two-phase Incompressible Inductionless MHD
authors: Bijie Song, Lingxiao Li, Jie Zhang
abstract: In this paper, we develop a robust augmented block preconditioner for three-dimensional, two-phase, incompressible inductionless MHD equations. We employ a high-order monolithic and charge-conservative arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) finite element method as base scheme, for which the solution variables are current density, velocity, electric potential and pressure. Grad-div stabilization is added in both the current density equation and discrete momentum equation. Backward Euler method is used for the time discretization. At each time step, fully coupled solution strategy is adopted. This leads to large-scale, ill-conditioned, nonsymmetric, and indefinite dual saddle-point system. To solve this system efficiently, we construct an augmented block preconditioner within the constraint preconditioning framework. The ultimate preconditioner combines the augmented Lagrangian technique with approximate block factorization for current density sub-system and fluid sub-system. The fully coupled four-field system is then solved using preconditioned FGMRES iteration. Numerical experiments confirm the high-order accuracy and discrete charge conservation of the ALE-FEM. Drop of heavy fluid in light fluid is taken as benchmark to demonstrate the robustness of the preconditioner with respect to the discontinuity of physical parameters and the mesh size.

infographic.key_insight: An augmented block preconditioner enables robust iterative solution of fully coupled, two-phase incompressible inductionless MHD systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports three-dimensional conducting-fluid simulations with discontinuous material properties and challenging coupled flow–current dynamics.
method: Discretize current density, velocity, electric potential and pressure using high-order, charge-conservative ALE finite elements and backward Euler time stepping.
Add grad-div stabilization to the current-density and momentum equations.
Combine augmented Lagrangian techniques with approximate block factorization, then solve using preconditioned FGMRES.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments confirm high-order accuracy and discrete charge conservation; a heavy-fluid-drop benchmark demonstrates preconditioner robustness to material-property discontinuities and mesh size.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract gives no quantitative iteration counts or runtime scaling, limiting assessment of computational efficiency.
infographic.paper_title: Robust augmented Block Preconditioning for two-phase Incompressible Inductionless MHD

title: Beyond Parameter Protection: Fisher-Shaped EWC for Replay-Free Continual Learning
authors: Liying Wang, Simone Magistri, Joost van de Weijer
abstract: In replay-free continual learning, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) uses Fisher information matrix (FIM) to protect acquired knowledge by penalizing changes to historically important parameters. However, a local importance estimate at the retained solution does not in general characterize sensitivity after finite parameter displacement. This motivates controlling Fisher sensitivity over a neighborhood of potential future updates. We propose Fisher-Shaped EWC (FS-EWC), which extends the role of FIM from parameter protection to solution formation for future retention. During task learning, FS-EWC minimizes the worst-case empirical FIM trace within a prescribed neighborhood, explicitly favoring solutions that are less sensitive to bounded future displacement. At task completion, trajectory-based model merging constructs the retained solution from multiple optimization states rather than a single terminal iterate, after which FIM is estimated for subsequent consolidation. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that FS-EWC improves performance over EWC, while controlled studies indicate a more favorable stability--plasticity balance and greater tolerance to parameter drift. These results suggest that effective knowledge retention requires both forming solutions with future retention in mind and protecting acquired knowledge.

infographic.key_insight: FS-EWC goes beyond protecting important parameters by shaping solutions to reduce Fisher sensitivity to bounded future parameter changes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For continually updated engineering models, this approach could help retain earlier learned behavior without replaying past data, though solid-mechanics validation is not reported in the abstract.
method: Minimize worst-case empirical Fisher information trace within a prescribed parameter neighborhood during task learning.
Merge multiple optimization states into a retained solution at task completion.
Estimate Fisher information at the merged solution for subsequent EWC consolidation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Multiple benchmark experiments report improvements over EWC, while controlled studies indicate a better stability–plasticity balance and greater tolerance to parameter drift.
infographic.watch_item: Neighborhood-based optimization and trajectory merging may add computational cost; the abstract does not quantify this overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Parameter Protection: Fisher-Shaped EWC for Replay-Free Continual Learning

title: Structure-preserving discretisations for the quasi-incompressible, thermal Maxwell-Stefan equations
authors: Boris D. Andrews, Aaron Baier-Reinio, Aaron Brunk, Patrick E. Farrell, Mária Lukáčová-Medviďová
abstract: We study a thermal Maxwell-Stefan-Navier-Stokes system modelling miscible mixtures under a quasi-incompressibility constraint. The system consists of the conservation laws for mass and momentum, and the balance law for entropy, which is preferred over the balance law for energy because it facilitates the development of two structure-preserving discretisation methods. The first method applies a semi-implicit Euler scheme in time, together with suitable finite elements in space, which guarantees generation of entropy and enforces the quasi-incompressibility constraint pointwise, but numerically dissipates total energy. The second method employs a continuous Petrov-Galerkin discretisation in time, which also generates entropy and satisfies the constraint pointwise, and in addition conserves the total energy and allows high-order time approximations. The structure-preserving properties and behaviour of both numerical methods are demonstrated by a series of numerical experiments.

infographic.key_insight: Two structure-preserving discretisations generate entropy and enforce quasi-incompressibility pointwise, while only the continuous Petrov–Galerkin method also conserves total energy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These methods support physically consistent simulation of coupled heat transfer, multicomponent diffusion, and fluid motion in miscible mixtures.
method: Model thermal Maxwell–Stefan–Navier–Stokes dynamics using mass, momentum, and entropy balances.
Combine semi-implicit Euler time stepping with suitable spatial finite elements.
Use continuous Petrov–Galerkin time discretisation for energy conservation and high-order temporal approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments demonstrate the structure-preserving properties and behaviour of both methods; the abstract reports no quantitative accuracy or efficiency metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The semi-implicit Euler method numerically dissipates total energy, which may matter for long-time thermal simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Structure-preserving discretisations for the quasi-incompressible, thermal Maxwell-Stefan equations
